children: By Christine Ji and Aditi Shrikant
Tim Cook may be stepping down as Apple's CEO, but he's sticking around in an expanded board role
As John Ternus, right, takes over the CEO role, Tim Cook will assume the role of executive chairman on Apple's board.
Congratulations, you've just scored a big promotion at work.

But the pay bump and more prestigious title comes with challenges. How do you delegate the tasks you formerly did, lead former peers and juggle increased responsibilities? To make things more complicated, how do you lean into your new role when your old boss is watching you from the wings and still making decisions?

These are questions that Apple's new CEO John Ternus will need to navigate as he takes over the reins from Tim Cook. Meanwhile, Cook is assuming the role of executive chairman on Apple's board, where he'll "assist with certain aspects of the company, including engaging with policymakers around the world," according to Apple (AAPL).

The stakes are particularly high this time around as the company undergoes an artificial-intelligence transition with the upcoming rollout of its Apple Intelligence and agentic Siri. Supply-chain constraints with memory chips and Apple's custom silicon are further complicating Apple's roadmap.

Ternus, who previously served as Apple's hardware chief, offers a different skillset than the operations-focused Cook. Investors and Apple enthusiasts alike are hoping that Ternus can introduce more innovative products with accompanying on-device AI capabilities.

A fresh-faced CEO who's more product-focused will be a good fit for Apple at a time when people are expecting new form factors to meet their AI demands, Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights and Strategy, told MarketWatch.

The 51-year-old Ternus is considered young for a CEO. In fact, he's a full decade younger than the average CEO, according to data from Korn Ferry. While Ternus's relative youth gives him a long horizon to steer Apple through its next technological transformation, it could also point to gaps in geopolitical and boardroom experience. That's where Cook's position as executive chair will come in handy.
"Tim Cook is not going away," Sag said.

Cook's new role likely involves managing Apple's existing relationship with the Trump administration and other administrative issues that don't directly affect product teams, Sag said. Cook has cultivated a delicate relationship with Trump over the past decade which has helped the iPhone maker secure key tariff exemptions. Apple has also pledged multi-year investments in domestic manufacturing.
Representatives from Apple did not immediately respond to MarketWatch's request for comment.

Preserving these relationships will require careful transition planning. Sag characterized Cook's ongoing involvement as "on-the-job training" for Ternus. "Ternus wasn't meeting with heads of state or anything like that," Sag said. "That's something where they'll work together and Ternus will gain those capabilities with time."

Apple has already been putting Ternus in the spotlight in the months leading up to the transition. Ternus introduced Apple's MacBook Neo back in March, and he's made appearances on Apple's past two earnings calls.
A ramp-up period is necessary
Apple's CEO succession plan is a textbook case of standard corporate protocol, according to organizational experts.
One of the "most expensive ways" to lose an employee is to promote them but not let them make any decisions, said workplace performance expert Henna Pryor.

To avoid this, many companies have a "ramp-up" period where executives gradually hand off their responsibilities, something it seems like Cook and Ternus have been doing for months. Apple announced the leadership transition back in April.

It's not natural or reasonable to expect a person's job to change overnight. "When I'm passing off my job to a new person it's really not just saying you've been promoted," she said. "It's saying which decisions are being transferred on day one and which responsibilities are transferring over after a defined ramp-up period."

For Apple, the stakes are particularly high. "CEO transitions are always a risk," namely for companies "that are driven by a singular vision," Morningstar chief equity market strategist Michael Field said. "That was the perception from investors with Steve Jobs and Tim Cook."

"It's a way of not shocking the market," Field said of Apple's CEO transition plan. Cook can provide guidance in the background, while Ternus can provide a fresh face and more hardware expertise, Field explained.

However, Field cautioned that this approach could have downsides: "You can argue as well that it's the worst of both worlds," he said. "If you replace someone but you don't give them full reins to do whatever they want, then you're not really going to get that growth."

It's also important not to assign any meaning to a boss's actions before talking to them, said Tessa West, a psychology professor at New York University and author of the book "Jerks at Work." Oftentimes these seemingly overbearing monitoring has nothing to do with how much someone trusts us.
"We often jump into conversations with the cause [of the behaviors] in mind instead of asking about a behavior itself," she said. "You do not have insight into all causes of someone's behavior."
Employees should have an open and clear line of communication about what actions will improve workflow and productivity, without making any assumption about perception of competency.
"Make it about the action," West said. "Don't make it about how the action makes you feel."
-Christine Ji -Aditi Shrikant
